yes_case.case: The structural friction that stands in the way of a Senate confirmation is primarily procedural: committee referral, holds, floor scheduling by leadership, and potential debate filibusters. However, the constitutional and procedural architecture of the U.S. Senate heavily favors the majority party's ability to overcome these frictions when the executive branch prioritizes a nominee. Procedural roadblocks such as committee bottlenecks and individual senator holds are routinely bypassed or overridden by cloture motions and majority-party floor control. Historical baseline data on cabinet and agency head confirmations indicates that when nominations reach the Senate floor under unified or determined leadership, procedural friction successfully prevents confirmation in only a small fraction of cases. Therefore, the structural friction present does not reliably stop a confirmation process once initiated by the executive.

When structural friction of this institutional magnitude is applied to a high-stakes agency head nomination, it successfully prevents a recorded floor vote the vast majority of the time.
